Transfer question · M00-LG1

Which uncertainty should guide her narrow start?

A researcher can build cheap voice tools after a technical breakthrough. She aims to serve every trade, starting with plumbers. No plumber has described losing work through missed calls.

B. Name the customer belief behind the first narrow market.

An opening makes the idea possible. It does not establish that plumbers have a costly problem or will pay to change how they handle calls.

  1. AExpansion can wait until the team understands the first trade.
  2. BLost jobs identify a customer assumption she can investigate before choosing a remedy.
  3. CTranscription accuracy tests technical performance. Customers might already recover every missed call.

What would change this? If plumbers already pay for missed-call handling, investigate what their current remedy leaves unsolved before proposing another.

Transfer question · M00-LG1

Which assumption should the founders have tested?

A team built a booking tool for music teachers. Teachers praised it but kept their paper diaries. Revenue never covered hosting, and the founders closed it when their savings ran out.

A. Test whether the paper diary causes a problem worth changing.

Savings ran out last. The earlier uncertainty was whether teachers had a costly problem that made switching worth the effort.

  1. AThis tests whether the customer has a costly enough problem to change behaviour.
  2. BEase of learning matters once the tool solves something worth changing. It does not establish that need.
  3. CA discovery channel can bring teachers to the tool without making paper bookings costly enough to replace.

What would change this? If teachers already paid and left only after repeated outages, investigate reliability before questioning the original need.

No market need in 42% of the post-mortems Start from a problem, not from your technology

Transfer question · M00-LG2

Which belief can a florist check against last week's orders?

A founder wants to build voice ordering for florists. She has seen staff answer calls while arranging bouquets, but has not asked what happens to those orders.

C. Test whether the interruption loses order details.

A problem hypothesis names people, a situation and an obstacle. It can lose without anyone trying the proposed product.

  1. AThis selects the remedy before establishing the problem.
  2. BA preference invites agreement without identifying a past cost.
  3. CA florist can describe a recent loss or show that none occurred.

What would change this? If recent order records show no lost details, investigate another obstacle instead of preserving the voice-ordering idea.

Write hypotheses a stranger could prove wrong
Fictional scenario for this learning check.
Transfer question · M00-LG2

What should the organiser do with this evidence?

A wardrobe organiser hears renters describe moving costs. Several share packing lists and ask for another conversation. Nobody has paid or received an offer.

B. Use the signal to choose what to test next.

Shared records and follow-up interest help explain a problem. They do not show that the people will pay for this offer.

  1. AHelping with research does not establish how many renters will buy.
  2. BThe lists identify problems worth testing with an offer, without establishing a sale.
  3. CA working-service demonstration could test use once the offer is defined. The current evidence can first sharpen which problem that offer addresses.

What would change this? If a renter pays for the offered service, record that payment separately from the earlier research signals.

It's a signal until somebody pays What backs your idea today?
Fictional scenario for this learning check.
Transfer question · M00-LG3

What should the team do first this week?

A team thinks small bakeries discard bread because nearby buyers hear about leftovers too late. A baker will let them try a same-day offer tomorrow. No software exists.

C. Run the real offer before building its delivery system.

Start with what you need to learn. A manual offer reaches real people and tests whether timely access changes what they do.

  1. AA stock dashboard addresses bakery operations before testing the uncertain buyer response.
  2. BSimulated reactions can help prepare a test, but cannot show what real buyers do.
  3. CA same-day offer tests the uncertain response using bread that really exists.

What would change this? If buyers already order but the bakery cannot identify available stock, test that stock handoff next.

The candid rule

Hit every goal? Then they were too small

Share of goals reached over several cycles, partly counts half, to scale. Zones are a rule of thumb

Share of goals reached · 0 to 100%
Too big, or off focus
Stretching
Sweet spot
Good
Too smallsandbagging
0%34%60%70%80%100%

Hit them all? You set them too small. Nobody checks your goals but you, so aim at two in three.

Sandbagging after Seibel and Caldwell, YC, Setting smarter goals. The sweet spot is Google's rule of thumb for stretch goals (re:Work), not a research finding. Zone limits from the course's group tracker.
The one question

Every two weeks, the same question

Asked by your group, answered with a number

Harkin, B., et al. (2016). Psychological Bulletin, reported against private progress. Cai, J., & Szeidl, A. (2018). Quarterly Journal of Economics. The two-week rhythm follows YC's group office hours (Alströmer, 2023, Lenny's Podcast).

The workshop ladder

Your work climbs five rungs toward real users

Your results are for users to interact with

"From concept to landing page, to product, to revenue".
A very good result is a growing startup

Work on what you control

Things you can control

  • Talk to 15 users each week
  • Present your progress every week and ask for help
  • Offer critical feedback and questions
  • Be an expert in your problem space
  • Pivot when you hit a brick wall

Things you can't totally control

  • Steady growth on your landing page
  • A lead list of potential users
  • Paying customers
"15 to 20 users" set to the homework's 15, "3 times" to every week.
How we work together

Coachability, accountability, bias to action. Or be elsewhere

1

Together we grow: coachability

We give candid and productive feedback. We listen and seek to understand.

2

We act as we say: accountability

We stick to our word where it's in our hands. We learn from failures where it's not.

3

Give first, dream first: bias to action

We prefer building and experimenting over understanding every aspect.

Transfer question · M00-LG4

Which comparison should lead her read-out?

A founder targeted conversations with venue managers. She held some, missed the rest because messages reached reception, and learned who controls booking. She wants introductions next week.

A. Lead with target and actual, then name the access gap.

The room can act on a specific request grounded in what happened. Activity totals and forecasts do not explain the missed target.

  1. ATarget against held conversations makes the progress gap visible. She can then explain the access problem and ask for manager introductions.
  2. BAn outreach trend can diagnose activity, but does not report whether the intended conversations happened.
  3. CA growth forecast does not explain this week's missed conversations or the help needed.

What would change this? If introductions already reach managers but calls reveal no problem, ask for help interpreting that evidence instead.

Module 00 · Workshop · 90 minutes

Workshop: Autopsy your startup before it dies

Find what could kill your idea, write hypotheses you can lose, and reach real people today.

What kills startups, and what will this course demand from you?

Workshop · step 1 of 3

Autopsy your own startup

1STEP 1 · 25 MIN

AUTOPSY YOUR OWN STARTUP

Find the customer assumption that kills your idea

  • Your starting point in one line
  • One year on, your startup is dead. Why?
  • Each cause becomes "We assumed …"
  • Circle the riskiest untested one
  • Pairs: "How do you know?"

Output Riskiest untested assumption, in your AssumptionsMinutes 25

Photo: StockSnap on Pixabay.
Workshop · step 2 of 3

Write hypotheses you can lose

2STEP 2 · 25 MIN

WRITE HYPOTHESES YOU CAN LOSE

Hypotheses a stranger could prove wrong

  • 3 hypotheses: who, problem, situation, workaround, cost
  • Rate the evidence: opinion, anecdote, conversation, payment
  • Rank them, riskiest first, start AI deep research
  • Kill line logged before any contact

Output 3 ranked hypotheses, their evidence, a kill lineMinutes 25

Photo: congerdesign on Pixabay.
Workshop · step 3 of 3

Reach real people, then commit

3STEP 3 · 40 MIN

REACH REAL PEOPLE, THEN COMMIT

Leave with the week already moving

  • 10 min: pick named people from your research
  • 15 min: 5 messages to named people, or one call
  • Don't name your problem, do NOT pitch
  • 10 min: floor or full bar, midweek pace
  • 5 min: your problem space in one sentence, find teammates

Output Messages sent, target, pace, possible teammatesMinutes 40

Photo: StockSnap on Pixabay.
